cards.front: How do you decide between inheritance and composition for two related classes?
cards.back: Ask whether the new class is a **kind of** the old one (is-a, so use inheritance) or **contains** one (has-a, so use composition). Name the relationship and one consequence for changing the code.
A **reference** is a value held in a variable or attribute that identifies where an object is stored in memory. It works like an address that tells the program where to look.
cards.hint: Think about how a program finds an object.

cards.front: What does it mean to override a method?
cards.back: To **override** a method, a subclass defines a method with the same name as an inherited one, so objects of the subclass use the new version instead of the inherited version.
cards.hint: Compare the subclass version with the inherited one.

cards.front: How do Loan and Book objects cooperate in a library system?
cards.back: They form an **association**: a Loan object calls a method of a Book object, such as getTitle, to use the Book's data.
cards.hint: Name both classes and the method call that links them.

cards.back: **Composition** is a design in which a class has attributes that are objects of other classes, forming a has-a relationship, such as a Car that has an Engine.
cards.hint: Think about the whole and its parts.

cards.front: What are the steps to design a Car that starts its Engine?
cards.back: 1. Engine has running, set to false by its constructor. 2. Engine.start sets running to true. 3. Car has an engine attribute, created in its constructor. 4. Car.start calls engine.start().
**Inheritance** lets a new class take the attributes and methods of an existing class, so it reuses code instead of repeating it. It models an is-a relationship.
cards.hint: Think about a Car and a Vehicle.

cards.front: What is the difference between a superclass and a subclass?
cards.back: The **superclass** is the existing class whose attributes and methods are inherited. The **subclass** is the new class that inherits them and may add or override features.

cards.front: Why does a change in a superclass matter for its subclasses?
cards.back: Changes made in the **superclass** are available to every subclass, so subclasses avoid repeating code that the superclass already holds.
cards.hint: Think about one change reaching many classes.

cards.front: After s1 = new Student('Ben', 10), then s2 = s1, then s2.setGrade(11), what is s1.grade?
cards.back: **11**. The assignment copies the reference, so s1 and s2 refer to the same Student object, and setGrade changes that one object.
cards.hint: Do s1 and s2 point to one object or two?

cards.front: A student writes s2 = s1 and thinks they now have two separate objects. What is wrong?
cards.back: Assigning one object variable to another does **not** make a new object. Both names refer to the same object, so changing one changes the other.
cards.hint: Copying a reference is not the same as copying the object.

cards.front: Bicycle extends Vehicle and overrides move to output pedalling. What is the output of b.move() where b = new Bicycle()?
cards.back: **pedalling**. Bicycle defines its own move, so the program uses that version rather than the inherited one in Vehicle.
cards.hint: Which move version does the object use?

cards.front: Should Bicycle and Wheel use inheritance or composition, and why?
cards.back: **Composition**. A bicycle has wheels and is not a kind of wheel, so this is a has-a relationship.
cards.hint: Ask whether it is is-a or has-a.

cards.front: How does a change to a superclass compare with a change to a part in composition?
cards.back: With **inheritance**, a superclass change affects all subclasses. With **composition**, a change in a part stays contained, and a part can be replaced with less effect.
cards.hint: Think about how tightly the classes are linked.
